items.q: What is the probability of getting a head on a fair coin?
hints: There are 2 equally likely outcomes on a coin, and 1 of them is a head.
1 favourable outcome out of 2 possible outcomes.

items.q: What is the probability of rolling a 4 on a fair six-sided die?
hints: There are 6 equally likely outcomes on a die, and only 1 of them is a 4.
1 favourable outcome out of 6 possible outcomes.

items.q: If P(A) = 0.35, find P(not A).
hints: Use P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

items.q: Can a probability be greater than 1?
hints: Recall the valid range for any probability.
Probabilities always lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), inclusive.
No

items.q: The probability of rain is 0.2. Write this as a percentage.
hints: Multiply the decimal probability by 100 to convert to a percentage.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Find P(red).
hints: P(red) = number of red counters / total counters.

items.q: If P(A) = 3/8, find P(not A).
hints: Use P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

items.q: How many outcomes are there when two fair coins are tossed?
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for each coin together.

items.q: List the sample space size for rolling a die and flipping a coin.
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for the die and for the coin.

items.q: How many outcomes are there when two six-sided dice are rolled?
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for each die together.

items.q: A spinner has 5 equal sections. It is spun twice. How many outcomes are there?
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for each spin together.

items.q: How many outcomes are there when a die is rolled three times?
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for each roll together.

items.q: A card is chosen from 4 cards labelled A, B, C, D and a coin is tossed. How many outcomes?
hints: Multiply the number of outcomes for the card choice and for the coin toss.

items.q: A meal deal has 4 sandwich choices, 3 drink choices, and 2 snack choices. How many different meal combinations are possible?
hints: Multiply the number of choices for each part of the meal together.

items.q: Can two mutually exclusive events happen together?
hints: Recall the definition of mutually exclusive events.
Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common, so they can't both happen.
No

items.q: If two events are independent, does one affect the probability of the other?
hints: Recall the definition of independent events.
Independent events don't influence each other's probability at all.
No

items.q: Are getting a head and getting a tail on one coin toss mutually exclusive?
hints: Check whether both outcomes could happen on the same single toss.
A single coin toss gives either a head or a tail, never both.
Yes

items.q: Are rolling a 3 and rolling an odd number on one die mutually exclusive?
hints: Check whether the two events share any common outcome.
Rolling a 3 is itself one of the odd numbers, so the events overlap.
No

items.q: Are tossing a coin and rolling a die independent events?
hints: Check whether the outcome of one affects the probabilities of the other.
The coin result has no bearing on the die result, or vice versa.
Yes

items.q: If events A and B are mutually exclusive, what is P(A and B)?
hints: Think about what 'mutually exclusive' means for two events happening together.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time, so their overlap is impossible.

items.q: Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. Find P(A or B).
hints: For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

items.q: A coin is tossed twice. Find the probability of two heads.
hints: For independent events, multiply the individual probabilities.

items.q: A die is rolled twice. Find the probability of getting a 6 both times.
hints: For independent events, multiply the individual probabilities.

items.q: Two independent events have probabilities 0.3 and 0.5. Find the probability both occur.
hints: For independent events, multiply the individual probabilities.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 3 blue counters. Two counters are chosen with replacement. Find P(red then red).
hints: With replacement, the probability stays the same each time — multiply it by itself.
P(red) = 2/5 each time, so (2/5) x (2/5).

items.q: Find the probability of choosing an ace from a pack and then rolling an even number.
hints: For independent events, multiply the individual probabilities.

items.q: A spinner lands on green with probability 0.4. It is spun twice. Find P(green both times).
hints: For independent events, multiply the individual probabilities.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are chosen without replacement. Find P(red then red).
items.imageAlt: A probability tree diagram. A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters, chosen without replacement. The first stage shows P(red)=3/5, P(blue)=2/5; the second stage probabilities change depending on the first choice. The path for red then red is highlighted.
items.imageCaption: Chosen without replacement — second stage changes.
hints: Without replacement, the second probability changes because one counter is already gone.
P(first red) = 3/5, P(second red) = 2/4, so (3/5) x (2/4).

items.q: A bag has 1 red and 3 blue counters. One counter is chosen, replaced, then another is chosen. Find P(red then blue).
items.imageAlt: A probability tree diagram. A bag has 1 red and 3 blue counters, chosen with replacement. Each stage shows P(red)=1/4 and P(blue)=3/4. The path for red then blue is highlighted.
hints: Follow the tree diagram branch: multiply along the red-then-blue path.

items.q: A fair coin is tossed twice. What is the probability of exactly one head?
items.imageAlt: A probability tree diagram for a fair coin tossed twice, each branch probability 1/2. The two paths giving exactly one head, HT and TH, are highlighted.
items.imageCaption: Highlighted: the outcomes with exactly one head.
hints: List the two branches that give exactly one head (HT and TH) and add their probabilities.

items.q: A bag has 2 red and 1 green counter. One is chosen with replacement twice. Find P(two greens).
hints: Follow the tree diagram branch: multiply along the green-then-green path.
P(green) = 1/3 each time, so (1/3) x (1/3).

items.q: A die is rolled twice. Find the probability of getting an odd number both times.
hints: Follow the tree diagram branch: multiply along the odd-then-odd path.
P(odd) = 1/2 each time, so (1/2) x (1/2).

items.q: A spinner has equal sections red, blue, blue. It is spun twice. Find P(red then red).
hints: Follow the tree diagram branch: multiply along the red-then-red path.
P(red) = 1/3 each time, so (1/3) x (1/3).

items.q: A bag has 4 black and 1 white counter. With replacement, find P(one black then one white).
hints: Follow the tree diagram branch: multiply along the black-then-white path.

items.q: A coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability of at least one head.
hints: It's easier to find P(no heads at all) first, then subtract from 1.
P(no heads) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8, so P(at least one head) = 1 - 1/8.

items.q: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability of exactly 2 heads.
items.imageAlt: A probability tree diagram for a fair coin tossed three times, showing all eight outcomes. The three outcomes with exactly two heads, HHT, HTH and THH, are highlighted.
items.imageCaption: Each branch has probability 1/2. Highlighted: exactly two heads.
hints: Count the number of ways to choose which 2 tosses are heads, then multiply by the probability of one such arrangement.

items.q: A biased coin has P(heads) = 0.6. It is tossed twice. Find the probability of exactly 1 head.
hints: Count the number of ways to get exactly 1 head, then multiply by the probability of one such arrangement.

items.q: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of exactly 3 heads.
hints: Count the number of ways to choose which 3 tosses are heads, then multiply by the probability of one such arrangement.

items.q: A biased coin has P(heads) = 0.3. Find the probability of no heads in 3 tosses.
hints: No heads means every toss is a tail — multiply the tail probability by itself 3 times.

items.q: A die is rolled 3 times. Find the probability of rolling exactly one 6.
hints: Count the number of ways to choose which roll is the 6, then multiply by the probability of one such arrangement.

items.q: For n independent trials with success probability p, how many ways can exactly k successes occur?
hints: Recall the notation for 'choose k from n' used in the binomial probability formula.
The number of arrangements is given by the binomial coefficient.
C(n,k)
